leaf_note: Fifth/Sixth Schedule administration is a constitutional provision for STs; M1B.5.4/1 (73rd Amendment) is not tested.
micro_topic: Scheduled & Tribal areas > Fifth Schedule Para 5 > Governor's power to exclude laws
core_fact: Under Para 5(1) of the Fifth Schedule the Governor may by public notification direct that an Act of Parliament or of the State Legislature shall not apply (or apply with modifications) to a Scheduled Area; Para 5(2) lets him make regulations, incl. on land transfer; Para 7 / Para 21 let Parliament amend the Schedules by ordinary law (not an Art. 368 amendment).

statements.label: opt1
statements.text: Provisions for the administration of Tribal areas are found in the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution.

phrases.meaning_here: tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram (Art. 244(2))

statements.label: opt2
statements.text: The Governor is not authorized to direct that any particular Act of Parliament or of the State Legislature shall not apply to a Scheduled Area.

phrases.meaning_here: denies a power the Governor has

phrases.phrase: Act of Parliament or of the Legislature of a State
phrases.meaning_here: both kinds of law can be excluded/modified

statements.true_fact: The Governor may by public notification direct that any Act of Parliament or of the State Legislature shall not apply, or apply with exceptions, to a Scheduled Area.

statements.label: opt3
statements.text: The Governor is authorized to make regulations to prohibit or restrict the transfer of land in a Tribal (Scheduled) area.
statements.decisive_phrase: prohibit or restrict the transfer of land

phrases.meaning_here: Para 5(2) regulations for peace and good government
by or among STs in the Scheduled Area

statements.label: opt4
statements.text: The provisions of the Constitution relating to the administration of Scheduled Areas and Tribes may be altered by Parliament by ordinary legislation.

phrases.meaning_here: simple-majority law, not deemed an Art. 368 amendment

statements.fact_source: Fifth Schedule Para 7(2); Sixth Schedule Para 21(2)

reconstruction.correct_statement: The Governor may direct that an Act of Parliament or of the State Legislature shall not apply to a Scheduled Area.
reconstruction.transformation: 'may direct' turned into 'is not authorized to direct'.
reconstruction.why: Para 5 gives the Governor wide legislative control over Scheduled Areas.
reconstruction.micro_topic_rule: Fifth Schedule: Governor can exclude/modify any law and make land-transfer regulations; Parliament amends the Schedule by ordinary law.

leaf_note: Appellate jurisdiction is judiciary structure, not judicial review.
micro_topic: Supreme Court > appellate jurisdiction > Arts 132-136
blueprint_keyword: Appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
core_fact: Art. 132: appeal in civil, criminal or other cases on a certified substantial question of constitutional interpretation; Art. 133: civil appeals on a substantial question of law of general importance; Art. 134(2): Parliament may by law enlarge criminal appellate jurisdiction (done by the 1970 Enlargement Act); Art. 136: special leave.

statements.label: opt1
statements.text: Appeal lies with the Supreme Court in cases involving interpretation of the Constitution — civil, criminal or others.

statements.label: opt2
statements.text: Appeal lies with the Supreme Court in civil cases irrespective of any constitutional question.

phrases.meaning_here: on a substantial question of law of general importance

statements.label: opt3
statements.text: The Supreme Court's power of granting special leave is limited and can be curtailed through a constitutional amendment.

phrases.meaning_here: Art. 136 can be changed only by amending the Constitution, not by ordinary law
phrases.note: 'limited' is loose: Art. 136 is very wide; the key treats the option as correct

statements.label: opt4
statements.text: Parliament has no power to make any law conferring on the Supreme Court further powers to hear appeals in criminal matters.
statements.fact_source: Art. 134(2); Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970
statements.true_fact: Art. 134(2) lets Parliament by law confer further criminal appellate powers on the SC (used in 1970).

reconstruction.correct_statement: Parliament may by law confer on the Supreme Court further powers to hear criminal appeals (Art. 134(2)).
reconstruction.why: Art. 134(2) is an express enabling clause.
reconstruction.micro_topic_rule: SC appellate: 132 constitutional, 133 civil, 134 criminal (+134(2) enlargement by Parliament), 136 special leave.

micro_topic: Federal vs unitary features > CAG
blueprint_keyword: Federal features of the Indian Constitution
core_fact: Federal features: written and rigid constitution, division of powers, supremacy of the Constitution, independent judiciary, bicameralism. The CAG audits both Union and State accounts under one integrated system - a unitary feature.

statements.label: opt1
statements.text: A rigid Constitution is a federal feature of the Indian Constitution.

phrases.meaning_here: federal provisions need special majority + ratification by half the states (Art. 368(2))

statements.label: opt2
statements.text: Distribution of powers is a federal feature of the Indian Constitution.

statements.label: opt3
statements.text: The Comptroller and Auditor General is a federal feature of the Indian Constitution.

phrases.meaning_here: single integrated audit of Union and States

statements.true_fact: The CAG (single integrated audit machinery for Union and States) is a unitary feature.

statements.label: opt4
statements.text: An independent Supreme Court is a federal feature of the Indian Constitution.

reconstruction.correct_statement: The CAG is a unitary, not a federal, feature.
reconstruction.transformation: A unitary institution placed in a federal list.
reconstruction.why: One CAG audits both levels, unlike a dual federal system.
reconstruction.micro_topic_rule: Unitary list: single citizenship, single constitution, integrated judiciary, All-India Services, CAG, Governor appointed by Centre, emergency provisions.

micro_topic: Constitutional bodies > Finance Commission (Art. 280) > functions
core_fact: Art. 280(3): the FC recommends (a) distribution of net tax proceeds between Union and States and among States, (b) principles for grants-in-aid from the Consolidated Fund of India, (c)/(bb) measures to augment State funds for local bodies, (d) any matter referred by the President in the interests of sound finance. It keeps no accounts.

statements.label: opt1
statements.text: The Finance Commission recommends the sharing of net proceeds of taxes between the Centre and States.

statements.label: opt2
statements.text: The Finance Commission recommends the principles governing grants-in-aid to the States by the Centre.

phrases.meaning_here: Art. 275 grants out of the CFI

statements.label: opt3
statements.text: The Finance Commission makes recommendations on matters referred to it by the President in the interests of sound finance.
statements.decisive_phrase: referred to it by the President

phrases.phrase: referred to it by the President

statements.label: opt4
statements.text: The Finance Commission maintains the income and expenditure details of the Centre and State Governments.

phrases.would_be_correct_if: the body were the CGA / State Accountants General

statements.true_fact: The FC only recommends; accounts are kept by the Controller General of Accounts / Accountants General and audited by the CAG.

reconstruction.correct_statement: The FC recommends devolution and grants; it does not maintain government accounts.
reconstruction.transformation: An accounting function attributed to an advisory body.
reconstruction.why: FC is a quasi-judicial advisory body appointed every 5 years.
reconstruction.micro_topic_rule: FC = recommends (Art. 280(3)); accounts = CGA/AG; audit = CAG.

micro_topic: Subordinate judiciary > district judges > appointment (Art. 233)
core_fact: Art. 233(1): appointments, posting and promotion of district judges are made by the Governor of the State in consultation with the High Court exercising jurisdiction in that State.

statements.label: opt1
statements.text: Under Article 233, a district judge is appointed by the President in consultation with the High Court of the State concerned.

phrases.meaning_here: appoints SC/HC judges, not district judges
phrases.would_be_correct_if: the post were a High Court judge

phrases.phrase: in consultation with the High court

statements.true_fact: The Governor, not the President, appoints district judges.

statements.label: opt2
statements.text: Under Article 233, a district judge is appointed by the Governor of the State concerned in consultation with the High Court of that State.

phrases.phrase: in consultation with the High court

statements.label: opt3
statements.text: Under Article 233, a district judge is appointed by the Governor of the State concerned in consultation with the Chief Justice of India.

phrases.would_be_correct_if: the post were a High Court judge (with the HC CJ and State Governor)

statements.true_fact: Consultation is with the High Court, not the CJI.

statements.label: opt4
statements.text: Under Article 233, a district judge is appointed by the Collegium of the High Court.

phrases.would_be_correct_if: the post were a SC/HC judge (SC collegium)

statements.true_fact: The Governor appoints, consulting the High Court; no collegium appointment.

reconstruction.correct_statement: District judges are appointed by the Governor in consultation with the High Court (Art. 233).
reconstruction.why: Subordinate judiciary is a State matter under HC control (Arts 233-237).
reconstruction.micro_topic_rule: Art. 233: Governor + HC; Art. 234 other judicial officers: Governor + HC + State PSC; Art. 235 control: HC.

micro_topic: Electoral reforms > NOTA > year of introduction
core_fact: In PUCL v Union of India (27 Sep 2013) the SC directed a 'None of the Above' option; ECI added the NOTA button to EVMs from the Nov-Dec 2013 Assembly elections (Chhattisgarh, MP, Rajasthan, Delhi, Mizoram); first Lok Sabha use 2014.

statements.label: opt1
statements.text: The NOTA button was introduced in Electronic Voting Machines in 2009.

phrases.would_be_correct_if: the event were the 2009 Lok Sabha election without NOTA

statements.fact_source: PUCL v Union of India (27 Sep 2013); ECI instructions Oct 2013
statements.true_fact: NOTA was introduced in 2013 after the SC's PUCL judgment (27 Sep 2013); first used in the Nov-Dec 2013 Assembly elections.

statements.label: opt2
statements.text: The NOTA button was introduced in Electronic Voting Machines in 2014.

phrases.meaning_here: first Lok Sabha election with NOTA
phrases.would_be_correct_if: the question asked first Lok Sabha use

statements.fact_source: PUCL v Union of India (27 Sep 2013); ECI instructions Oct 2013
statements.true_fact: NOTA was introduced in 2013 after the SC's PUCL judgment (27 Sep 2013); first used in the Nov-Dec 2013 Assembly elections.

statements.label: opt3
statements.text: The NOTA button was introduced in Electronic Voting Machines in 2011.
statements.fact_source: PUCL v Union of India (27 Sep 2013); ECI instructions Oct 2013
statements.true_fact: NOTA was introduced in 2013 after the SC's PUCL judgment (27 Sep 2013); first used in the Nov-Dec 2013 Assembly elections.

statements.label: opt4
statements.text: The NOTA button was introduced in Electronic Voting Machines in 2013.
statements.fact_source: PUCL v Union of India (27 Sep 2013); ECI instructions Oct 2013

reconstruction.correct_statement: NOTA was introduced on EVMs in 2013.
reconstruction.why: Introduced by SC direction in Sep 2013.
reconstruction.micro_topic_rule: NOTA: SC 2013 (PUCL) -> first used Nov 2013 state polls -> Lok Sabha 2014; NOTA votes do not affect the result.

micro_topic: Election Commission > CEC vs ECs > powers; election disputes; rolls
core_fact: Art. 324: ECI has constitutional status and superintends electoral rolls and elections. Under the 1991 Act the CEC and ECs have equal powers and decide by majority (T.N. Seshan v UoI, 1995). Election disputes go to the HC/SC by election petition, not the ECI.

statements.label: opt1
statements.text: The members of the Election Commission do not have equal powers with the Chief Election Commissioner.

phrases.would_be_correct_if: the point were removal (CEC removable like an SC judge, ECs on CEC's recommendation)

statements.fact_source: Election Commission (CEC and Other ECs) Act 1991, s.10; T.N. Seshan v UoI (1995)
statements.true_fact: CEC and ECs have equal powers; decisions by majority (only removal protection differs).

statements.label: opt2
statements.text: Disputes related to elections are not decided by the Election Commission alone.
statements.decisive_phrase: not decided by the Election Commission only

phrases.meaning_here: HC under RPA 1951; SC for President/VP (Art. 71)

statements.label: opt3
statements.text: The Election Commission of India enjoys constitutional status.

statements.label: opt4
statements.text: Keeping the voters' list updated at all times is the responsibility of the Election Commission.

phrases.meaning_here: superintendence of preparation of electoral rolls

reconstruction.correct_statement: The Election Commissioners have equal powers with the CEC.
reconstruction.why: Multi-member ECI decides by majority.
reconstruction.micro_topic_rule: ECI: equal powers + majority decisions; only CEC has SC-judge-like removal protection.

micro_topic: Punchhi Commission > Arts 355/356 > localised emergency
core_fact: The Punchhi Commission (set up April 2007 by the UPA govt; report 2010) recommended amending Arts 355 and 356 to allow 'localised emergency' (district/part of State, max 3 months), fixed 5-year tenure for Governors and removal only by a State Legislature resolution; Governor should not have been in active politics for a couple of years before appointment.

statements.label: opt1
statements.text: The Punchhi Commission was constituted by the UPA government to study Centre-State relations.

statements.label: opt2
statements.text: The Commission recommended that a Governor nominee should not have participated in active politics for at least a couple of years before appointment.

statements.label: opt3
statements.text: The Commission recommended that there is no need to amend Articles 355 and 356.
statements.true_fact: Punchhi recommended amending Arts 355/356 to enable localised emergency for up to 3 months.

statements.label: opt4
statements.text: The Commission also criticised the arbitrary dismissal of Governors.

phrases.meaning_here: removal at the Centre's sweet will

statements.fact_source: Punchhi Report Vol II; B.P. Singhal v UoI (2010)

reconstruction.correct_statement: Punchhi recommended amending Arts 355 and 356 (localised emergency).
reconstruction.why: Its signature idea was a localised emergency.
reconstruction.micro_topic_rule: Punchhi (2007-10): localised emergency, 5-yr Governor tenure, Governor removal by state legislature, cooling-off for politicians.

micro_topic: Fundamental Rights > Art. 33 > armed forces
core_fact: Art. 33 empowers Parliament to restrict or abrogate FRs of the armed forces, para-military, police, intelligence agencies and allied forces (e.g. Army Act 1950).

statements.label: opt1
statements.text: The Fundamental Rights of members of the armed forces can be specifically restricted under Article 33.

phrases.meaning_here: Parliament's power to modify FRs of forces

statements.label: opt2
statements.text: The Fundamental Rights of members of the armed forces can be specifically restricted under Article 19.
statements.true_fact: Art. 19 is the freedoms; the restricting power for forces is Art. 33.

statements.label: opt3
statements.text: The Fundamental Rights of members of the armed forces can be specifically restricted under Article 21.
statements.true_fact: Art. 21 is life and liberty; forces restriction is Art. 33.

statements.label: opt4
statements.text: The Fundamental Rights of members of the armed forces can be specifically restricted under Article 25.
statements.true_fact: Art. 25 is religious freedom; forces restriction is Art. 33.

reconstruction.correct_statement: Art. 33 lets Parliament restrict FRs of the armed forces.
reconstruction.transformation: Article number swapped for rights articles.
reconstruction.why: Art. 33 is the only specific power.
reconstruction.micro_topic_rule: Arts 33 (forces), 34 (martial law), 35 (Parliament's exclusive law power).

leaf_note: Citizenship (Part II) - nearest leaf is Salient features.
micro_topic: Citizenship > Art. 11 > Parliament's power to regulate
core_fact: Art. 11: Parliament may make any provision for acquisition, termination and all other matters relating to citizenship (Citizenship Act 1955). Art. 10 only continues citizenship subject to such law; Art. 12 defines 'State'; Art. 13 voids laws inconsistent with FRs.

statements.label: opt1
statements.text: Article 10 empowers Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law.

phrases.meaning_here: continuance of citizenship 'subject to' Parliament's law
phrases.would_be_correct_if: the question asked continuance of rights

statements.true_fact: Art. 10 only continues citizenship subject to law; the power is Art. 11.

statements.label: opt2
statements.text: Article 11 empowers Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law.

phrases.meaning_here: Parliament to regulate citizenship by law

statements.label: opt3
statements.text: Article 12 empowers Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law.
statements.true_fact: Art. 12 defines 'State'.

statements.label: opt4
statements.text: Article 13 empowers Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law.
statements.true_fact: Art. 13 is judicial review of laws vs FRs.

reconstruction.correct_statement: Art. 11 empowers Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship.
reconstruction.transformation: Stem says 'rights of the citizens' (ambiguous), not 'right of citizenship'.
reconstruction.why: Art. 11 is the enabling clause of Part II.
reconstruction.micro_topic_rule: Part II: Arts 5-8 who is a citizen, 9 voluntary foreign citizenship, 10 continuance, 11 Parliament regulates.

key_note: Deleted by APPSC. Likely because 'rights of the citizens' does not equal 'right of citizenship' and Art. 10 also refers to Parliament's law. Truths verified from the text (basis fact).

micro_topic: Union executive > President > form of address
core_fact: 'His/Her Excellency' was the traditional form of address for the President (and Governors). Since 2012 (Pranab Mukherjee) 'Rashtrapati ji'/'Hon'ble President' is used domestically; 'Excellency' is kept for foreign dignitaries.

statements.label: opt1
statements.text: The correct form of address for the President of India is His Lordship.
statements.true_fact: 'Lordship' is a judicial address; the President is 'His Excellency'.

statements.label: opt2
statements.text: The correct form of address for the President of India is His Honour.
statements.true_fact: 'Honour' is for judges; the President is 'His Excellency'.

statements.label: opt3
statements.text: The correct form of address for the President of India is His Highness.
statements.true_fact: 'Highness' is for royalty; the President is 'His Excellency'.

statements.label: opt4
statements.text: The correct form of address for the President of India is His Excellency.

phrases.meaning_here: traditional address for the Head of State

reconstruction.correct_statement: The President was addressed as 'His Excellency'.
reconstruction.why: Protocol honorific for Heads of State.
reconstruction.micro_topic_rule: Excellency = President/Governor (now restricted to foreign protocol since 2012); Lordship/Honour = judges; Highness = royals.

key_note: Key kept. Note: since Oct 2012 'His Excellency' is no longer used for the President in Indian domestic usage, only in foreign protocol.

micro_topic: Rajamannar Committee > recommendations > Governor, Art 356, ISC, AIS
core_fact: The Rajamannar Committee (Tamil Nadu govt, 1969; report 1971) sought greater State autonomy: immediate creation of an Inter-State Council, omission/safeguards on Art. 356, abolition of the All-India Services (IAS, IPS), Governor's role to be curbed (no discretion; appointment in consultation with State).

statements.label: opt1
statements.text: The Rajamannar Committee recommended the creation of an Inter-State Council.

phrases.meaning_here: Art. 263 body to be set up at once

statements.label: opt2
statements.text: The Rajamannar Committee recommended curbing the misuse of Article 356.

phrases.meaning_here: it wanted Arts 356, 357, 365 omitted or safeguarded

statements.label: opt3
statements.text: The Rajamannar Committee recommended the abolition of the IAS and IPS.

phrases.meaning_here: All-India Services seen as central control

statements.label: opt4
statements.text: The Rajamannar Committee recommended strengthening the Governor system.
statements.true_fact: Rajamannar wanted the Governor's powers curbed and State autonomy increased.

reconstruction.correct_statement: Rajamannar wanted the Governor's role curbed, not strengthened.
reconstruction.why: A State-appointed committee arguing for autonomy cannot recommend a stronger central agent.
reconstruction.micro_topic_rule: Rajamannar (TN 1969): pro-State autonomy; Sarkaria (Centre 1983) and Punchhi (Centre 2007) are central commissions.

leaf_note: A judicial doctrine; judiciary leaf fits best.
micro_topic: Judicial doctrines > parens patriae
core_fact: Parens patriae ('parent of the nation'): the State acts as guardian of persons unable to protect themselves (minors, the mentally ill, disaster victims) - used in Charan Lal Sahu v UoI (1989, Bhopal) and Aruna Shanbaug (2011).

statements.label: opt1
statements.text: The doctrine of parens patriae means the authority regarded as the legal protector of citizens unable to protect themselves.

statements.label: opt2
statements.text: The doctrine of parens patriae means an inconsistency or contradiction between two or more parts of legal instruments.
statements.true_fact: Inconsistency between laws is repugnancy, not parens patriae.

statements.label: opt3
statements.text: The doctrine of parens patriae means Parliament has no power to make laws on any matter belonging to the States.

phrases.would_be_correct_if: the concept were distribution of legislative powers

statements.true_fact: That describes distribution of legislative competence, not parens patriae.

statements.label: opt4
statements.text: The doctrine of parens patriae means it is the duty of the court to interpret legislation made by Parliament.
statements.true_fact: Interpretation of statutes is a general judicial function, not parens patriae.

reconstruction.correct_statement: Parens patriae = the State as guardian of those who cannot protect themselves.
reconstruction.why: Latin 'parent of the country'.
reconstruction.micro_topic_rule: Match doctrine to definition: parens patriae (guardian), repugnancy (inconsistency), pith and substance (competence), eclipse, severability.

leaf_note: Paramountcy is part of constitutional development before 1947; app topic (Anglo-Maratha wars) is off.
micro_topic: British India > princely states > paramountcy > grounds of intervention
core_fact: Under paramountcy the princely states had internal autonomy but no international personality; the Crown intervened in internal affairs for misgovernment, to protect the state and to give effect to its international obligations (Butler Committee 1929).

statements.label: opt1
statements.text: The British never interfered in the internal administration of Indian states.
statements.fact_source: Butler Committee Report 1929; annexation of Awadh 1856
statements.true_fact: The paramount power did interfere (misgovernment, international commitments).

statements.label: opt2
statements.text: The British interfered in the internal administration of Indian states for giving effect to its international commitments.

phrases.meaning_here: states had no international life; the Crown answered for them

statements.label: opt3
statements.text: The British interfered in the internal administration of Indian states on the request of the Congress party.
statements.true_fact: Intervention was a Crown prerogative, never at Congress's request.

statements.label: opt4
statements.text: The British interfered in the internal administration of Indian states on the request of the people.
statements.true_fact: Intervention was a Crown prerogative, not at the people's request.

reconstruction.correct_statement: The Crown intervened in princely states to give effect to its international commitments.
reconstruction.why: Since states had no international personality, the Crown discharged treaty obligations for them.
reconstruction.micro_topic_rule: Paramountcy: internal autonomy, external control; intervention on misrule/international obligations.

micro_topic: Bicameral State legislature > Art. 169 > creation/abolition of Legislative Council
core_fact: Art. 169: Parliament may by law abolish or create a Legislative Council if the Legislative Assembly passes a resolution by a majority of its total membership and two-thirds of those present and voting; such a law is not deemed an amendment under Art. 368 (simple majority in Parliament).

statements.label: opt1
statements.text: The procedure to abolish or create a Legislative Council in a State is a constitutional amendment with simple majority.

phrases.would_be_correct_if: it said 'law of Parliament not deemed an amendment'

statements.true_fact: It is an ordinary law of Parliament (not deemed an Art. 368 amendment) after an Assembly resolution.

statements.label: opt2
statements.text: The procedure to abolish or create a Legislative Council in a State is a constitutional amendment by two-thirds majority.

phrases.meaning_here: the special majority belongs to the State Assembly resolution

statements.true_fact: The 2/3 (special) majority is the Assembly's; Parliament then passes an ordinary law.

statements.label: opt3
statements.text: A Legislative Council is abolished or created on a resolution of the State Legislature passed by a two-thirds majority, followed by an Act of Parliament.
statements.decisive_phrase: resolution with 2/3 majority, followed by an act of parliament

phrases.meaning_here: majority of total membership + 2/3 present and voting

statements.label: opt4
statements.text: Parliament directly creates or abolishes a Legislative Council by simple majority.

phrases.would_be_correct_if: the Assembly resolution had been passed first

statements.true_fact: Parliament can act only after the Assembly's special-majority resolution.

reconstruction.correct_statement: Assembly resolution (special majority) + Act of Parliament (Art. 169).
reconstruction.transformation: Procedure recast as an Art. 368 amendment or a direct Parliament power.
reconstruction.decisive: followed by an act of parliament
reconstruction.why: Art. 169 is a two-step State-initiated procedure.
reconstruction.micro_topic_rule: Art. 169: State Assembly special majority -> Parliament simple-majority law, not an Art. 368 amendment (AP Council abolished 1985, revived 2007).

micro_topic: President > electoral college (Art. 54) > Legislative Council excluded
core_fact: Art. 54: the President is elected by elected members of both Houses of Parliament and elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies (incl. Delhi and Puducherry, 70th Amendment). Members of Legislative Councils and nominated members do not vote.

statements.label: opt1
statements.text: A Chief Minister is not eligible to vote in the Presidential election if he is a Member of the Legislative Council of the State Legislature.
statements.decisive_phrase: Member of the Legislative Council of the State Legislature

statements.label: opt2
statements.text: A Chief Minister is not eligible to vote in the Presidential election if he is a Member of the Legislative Assembly of the State Legislature.
statements.decisive_phrase: Member of the Legislative Assembly of the State Legislature
statements.true_fact: Elected MLAs are in the electoral college.

statements.label: opt3
statements.text: A Chief Minister is not eligible to vote in the Presidential election if he is a Member of Lok Sabha.
statements.true_fact: Elected Lok Sabha members vote.

statements.label: opt4
statements.text: A Chief Minister is not eligible to vote in the Presidential election if he is a Member of Rajya Sabha.
statements.true_fact: Elected Rajya Sabha members vote.

reconstruction.correct_statement: A CM who is an MLC cannot vote in the Presidential election.
reconstruction.transformation: Houses in the electoral college offered.
reconstruction.why: MLCs are excluded from Art. 54.
reconstruction.micro_topic_rule: President's electoral college: elected MPs + elected MLAs (incl. Delhi, Puducherry); no MLCs, no nominated members; VP: all MPs.

micro_topic: Elections > types > mid-term election
core_fact: A mid-term election is held when a legislature is dissolved before completing its term; a by-election fills a single vacancy; a general election follows the normal expiry of the term.

statements.label: opt1
statements.text: An election held for a legislature dissolved before the expiry of its term is known as a by-election.
statements.true_fact: A by-election fills a casual vacancy.

statements.label: opt2
statements.text: An election held for a legislature dissolved before the expiry of its term is known as a mid-term election.

statements.label: opt3
statements.text: An election held for a legislature dissolved before the expiry of its term is known as a general election.
statements.true_fact: A general election follows expiry of the full term.

statements.label: opt4
statements.text: An election held for a legislature dissolved before the expiry of its term is known as a extraordinary election.
statements.true_fact: No 'extraordinary election' exists.

reconstruction.correct_statement: Election after premature dissolution = mid-term election.
reconstruction.why: Defined by timing of dissolution.
reconstruction.micro_topic_rule: By-election = one seat; mid-term = whole House early; general = full term.

micro_topic: Elections > EVM > vote capacity
core_fact: ECI: the EVM (M2 model, in use c. 2006-2017) can record a maximum of 3,840 votes; the later M3 EVM records up to 2,000 votes per control unit (polling stations have <1,500 voters).

statements.label: opt1
statements.text: The maximum number of votes that can be recorded by an EVM is 3840.

statements.label: opt2
statements.text: The maximum number of votes that can be recorded by an EVM is 4840.
statements.true_fact: The (M2-era) EVM could record a maximum of 3,840 votes.

statements.label: opt3
statements.text: The maximum number of votes that can be recorded by an EVM is 2840.
statements.true_fact: The (M2-era) EVM could record a maximum of 3,840 votes.

statements.label: opt4
statements.text: The maximum number of votes that can be recorded by an EVM is 3000.
statements.true_fact: The (M2-era) EVM could record a maximum of 3,840 votes.

reconstruction.correct_statement: An EVM can record up to 3,840 votes.
reconstruction.why: ECI technical specification at the time.
reconstruction.micro_topic_rule: EVM: 3,840 votes (M2), 64 candidates with 4 ballot units (M2), M3 up to 384 candidates with 24 BUs.

micro_topic: Judicial review > legislative response to SC rulings
core_fact: SC judgments bind all (Art. 141, 144), but the legislature may remove the basis of a judgment by a validating law or a constitutional amendment (e.g. 1st, 24th, 42nd Amendments), subject to basic structure; judges have security of tenure (Art. 124(4)).

statements.label: opt1
statements.text: When the Government and Legislature dislike a decision of the Supreme Court they can change the judges of the Supreme Court.

phrases.meaning_here: judges removable only for proved misbehaviour/incapacity

statements.true_fact: Judges have security of tenure; they cannot be removed for a ruling.

statements.label: opt2
statements.text: When the Government and Legislature dislike a decision of the Supreme Court they can ignore the decision.
statements.true_fact: SC decisions bind all authorities (Arts 141, 144).

statements.label: opt3
statements.text: When the Government and Legislature dislike a decision of the Supreme Court they can pass a constitutional amendment or a law to overcome it.
statements.decisive_phrase: Constitutional amendment or pass a law
statements.fact_source: Art. 368; Indra Sawhney/Madras Bar line on validating laws

statements.label: opt4
statements.text: The Supreme Court's decision is final and ultimate and cannot be challenged by the Government and Legislature.
statements.true_fact: A ruling binds but can be reviewed (Art. 137) or overcome by amendment/validating law.

reconstruction.correct_statement: Parliament can overcome an SC decision by amendment or validating law.
reconstruction.transformation: Legitimate route replaced by illegitimate or absolute ones.
reconstruction.decisive: Constitutional amendment or pass a law
reconstruction.why: Legislature can change the law on which a ruling rests, not the ruling's binding force.
reconstruction.micro_topic_rule: Overrule route = change the law (amendment/validating Act), never ignore or remove judges.

statements.true_fact: National Voters' Day is 25 January (ECI founded 25 Jan 1950), observed since 2011.

micro_topic: Sarkaria Commission > Governor > appointment criteria
core_fact: Sarkaria (1983-88) on Governors: eminent in some walk of life; from outside the State; detached figure not too intimately connected with local politics; not recently active in politics; secure 5-year term not cut short except for compelling reasons; CM to be consulted.

statements.text: The Sarkaria Commission recommended a secure five-year term for the Governor.

phrases.meaning_here: term not to be cut short except rarely

statements.label: opt2

phrases.phrase: not the native of a State

statements.label: opt3
statements.text: The Sarkaria Commission recommended that the Governor must be an eminent person in some field.

phrases.meaning_here: eminence in some walk of life

statements.fact_source: Sarkaria Report ch. IV; app notes

statements.label: opt4
statements.text: The Sarkaria Commission recommended that the Governor should have travelled extensively in and around the State.
statements.true_fact: Sarkaria laid down no travel criterion; its criteria were eminence, outsider, political detachment.

reconstruction.correct_statement: Sarkaria did not prescribe travel in the State as a criterion.
reconstruction.why: Not among the criteria.
reconstruction.micro_topic_rule: Sarkaria Governor criteria: eminent, outsider, detached, not recently in politics, CM consulted, secure term.

leaf_note: Model Code of Conduct is an electoral-reform topic; party-system leaf is not tested.
micro_topic: Model Code of Conduct > party in power > misuse of official machinery
core_fact: MCC Part VII ('Party in Power'): ministers shall not combine official visits with electioneering, shall not use official machinery or personnel, government vehicles, or announce grants/payments from discretionary funds once elections are announced.

statements.label: opt1
statements.text: Under the Model Code of Conduct the ruling party may use government servants to win voters in its favour.

phrases.would_be_correct_if: the stem asked what a ruling party misuses in practice

statements.fact_source: ECI Model Code of Conduct, Part VII
statements.true_fact: MCC bars the party in power from using government servants for electioneering.

statements.label: opt2
statements.text: Under the Model Code of Conduct the ruling party may use government vehicles to win voters in its favour.
statements.fact_source: ECI Model Code of Conduct, Part VII
statements.true_fact: MCC bars use of official vehicles for campaigning.

statements.label: opt3
statements.text: Under the Model Code of Conduct the ruling party may use discretionary grants to win voters in its favour.

phrases.meaning_here: sanctions from discretionary funds - barred after announcement

statements.fact_source: ECI Model Code of Conduct, Part VII
statements.true_fact: MCC bars ministers from sanctioning grants out of discretionary funds after polls are announced.

statements.label: opt4
statements.text: The ruling party may use its own political party organisation to win voters in its favour.

phrases.meaning_here: party machinery is a legitimate campaign resource

reconstruction.correct_statement: A ruling party may campaign through its party, but not through government servants, vehicles or discretionary grants.
reconstruction.transformation: Prohibited official resources presented as usable.
reconstruction.why: MCC separates party resources from State resources.
reconstruction.micro_topic_rule: MCC 'Party in Power': no official machinery, staff, vehicles, discretionary grants, new schemes or ad campaigns at public cost.

key_note: APPSC's final key accepted options 1, 2 and 3 (stored key = option 1). Read as 'resources the ruling party may not use under the MCC'; on a literal reading of the stem, option 4 would be the odd one. Key kept.

micro_topic: Inter-State relations > constitutional vs statutory bodies
core_fact: The Inter-State Council is provided for in Art. 263 (set up 1990). River water tribunals are statutory (Inter-State River Water Disputes Act 1956, under Art. 262); Zonal Councils are statutory (States Reorganisation Act 1956, s.15).

statements.label: opt1
statements.text: The River Water Tribunal is a constitutional body concerned with inter-State relations.
statements.true_fact: River water tribunals are statutory bodies (ISRWD Act 1956).

statements.label: opt2
statements.text: The Inter-State Council is a constitutional body concerned with inter-State relations.

statements.label: opt3
statements.text: The Zonal Council is a constitutional body concerned with inter-State relations.
statements.true_fact: Zonal Councils are statutory (SR Act 1956).

statements.label: opt4
statements.text: The Zonal Tribunal is a constitutional body concerned with inter-State relations.
statements.true_fact: No 'Zonal Tribunal' exists.

reconstruction.correct_statement: The Inter-State Council (Art. 263) is the constitutional body.
reconstruction.why: Only ISC is in the text of the Constitution.
reconstruction.micro_topic_rule: Constitutional: ISC (263); statutory: Zonal Councils (SRA 1956), river tribunals (ISRWD 1956), NE Council (1971).

micro_topic: Constituent Assembly > committees > Union Constitution Committee
core_fact: Major CA committees: Union Powers and Union Constitution Committees, States Committee - Jawaharlal Nehru; Drafting Committee - B.R. Ambedkar; Rules of Procedure, Steering - Rajendra Prasad; FR sub-committee - J.B. Kripalani; Advisory - Patel.

statements.label: opt1
statements.text: Dr B.R. Ambedkar was the Chairman of the Union Constitution Committee of the Constituent Assembly.
statements.true_fact: Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee; Nehru chaired the Union Constitution Committee.

statements.label: opt2
statements.text: Jawaharlal Nehru was the Chairman of the Union Constitution Committee of the Constituent Assembly.

phrases.meaning_here: chairman, Union Constitution / Union Powers / States Committees

statements.label: opt3

statements.true_fact: Kripalani chaired the Fundamental Rights sub-committee.

statements.label: opt4
statements.text: Rajendra Prasad was the Chairman of the Union Constitution Committee of the Constituent Assembly.
statements.true_fact: Prasad chaired the Rules of Procedure and Steering Committees.

reconstruction.correct_statement: Nehru chaired the Union Constitution Committee.
reconstruction.why: Nehru chaired the three 'Union/States' committees.
reconstruction.micro_topic_rule: Nehru: Union Powers, Union Constitution, States; Patel: Advisory, Provincial Constitution; Prasad: Steering, Rules; Ambedkar: Drafting.

micro_topic: Parliamentary control over administration > devices
core_fact: Legislative control tools: questions, zero hour, motions (adjournment, no-confidence, censure), resolutions, debates, committees. Dissolution of the House is an executive power (President on the PM's advice, Art. 85(2)(b)).

statements.label: opt1
statements.text: Questions are a tool of legislative control over the administration in India.

statements.label: opt2
statements.text: Resolutions are a tool of legislative control over the administration in India.

statements.label: opt3
statements.text: Dissolution of the House is a tool of legislative control over the administration in India.

phrases.would_be_correct_if: the tool were 'executive control over the legislature'

statements.true_fact: Dissolution is an executive power (President/Governor on advice), the reverse of legislative control.

statements.label: opt4
statements.text: The no-confidence motion is a tool of legislative control over the administration in India.

reconstruction.correct_statement: Dissolution is an executive weapon, not a legislative control device.
reconstruction.why: Executive dissolves the House; the House controls the executive by questions/motions.
reconstruction.micro_topic_rule: Legislative control = questions, motions, resolutions, committees; dissolution = executive control.

micro_topic: Nature of constitution > constitutionalism / rule of law
core_fact: Constitutional government (constitutionalism) means rule according to fixed, impersonal rules that bind all office-holders; rulers change, rules persist (rule of law).

statements.label: opt1
statements.text: 'Persons may change but rules should not change' is the principle of the republican form of government.

phrases.would_be_correct_if: the principle were elected head of State

statements.true_fact: Republic = elected/non-hereditary head of State.

statements.label: opt2
statements.text: 'Persons may change but rules should not change' is the principle of absolute monarchy.

phrases.meaning_here: rule by the will of a person

statements.true_fact: Absolute monarchy is rule by a person's will - the opposite.

statements.label: opt3
statements.text: 'Persons may change but rules should not change' is the principle of the socialist system.
statements.true_fact: Socialism concerns ownership of means of production.

statements.label: opt4
statements.text: 'Persons may change but rules should not change' is the principle of constitutional government.

reconstruction.correct_statement: Impersonal fixed rules = constitutional government.
reconstruction.why: Constitutionalism limits rulers by rules.
reconstruction.micro_topic_rule: Constitutionalism = rule of law, limited govt; republic = elected head; monarchy = hereditary.

micro_topic: Distribution of legislative powers > cow slaughter > source
core_fact: Art. 48 (DPSP) directs the State to prohibit slaughter of cows, calves and other milch and draught cattle. Legislative competence on preservation of stock is State List Entry 15; prevention of cruelty to animals is Concurrent List Entry 17 (basis of the Centre's 1960 Act and 2017 livestock-market rules).

statements.label: opt1
statements.text: The Central government legislates on cow slaughter under its emergency powers.

phrases.meaning_here: Art. 250 lets Parliament legislate on State subjects only during emergency

statements.true_fact: Emergency power is not the source; the key points to Art. 48.
statements.mechanism: true fact not the one asked

statements.label: opt2
statements.text: The Central government legislates on cow slaughter under Article 148.
statements.true_fact: Art. 148 concerns the CAG.

statements.label: opt3
statements.text: The Central government legislates on cow slaughter under Entry 17, List III (prevention of cruelty to animals).

phrases.meaning_here: Concurrent List: prevention of cruelty to animals
phrases.note: arguably the actual legislative head for central rules
phrases.would_be_correct_if: the question asked the legislative entry

statements.true_fact: The key treats Art. 48 (DPSP) as the source.
statements.mechanism: true fact not the one asked

statements.label: opt4

phrases.meaning_here: DPSP on organising agriculture and animal husbandry, prohibiting cow slaughter

reconstruction.why: Art. 48 is the only provision naming cow slaughter.
reconstruction.micro_topic_rule: Cow slaughter: Art. 48 (DPSP direction), Entry 15 List II (preservation of stock), Entry 17 List III (cruelty).

key_note: Key kept. Caveat: a DPSP is not a source of legislative power; Central rules (2017) were framed under the PCA Act 1960 (Entry 17, List III), so option 3 is defensible. APPSC's key = Art. 48.

micro_topic: Parliament > Rajya Sabha > seats of AP and Telangana after 2014
core_fact: Under the AP Reorganisation Act 2014 (s.12, amending the Fourth Schedule), the 18 Rajya Sabha seats of undivided AP were split: Andhra Pradesh 11, Telangana 7.

micro_topic: State legislature > Legislative Council > Art. 169
core_fact: Art. 169 provides for the abolition or creation of Legislative Councils in States (Art. 168 lists bicameral States; Art. 171 composition).

reconstruction.why: Creation/abolition clause.
reconstruction.micro_topic_rule: 168 (bicameral States), 169 (create/abolish), 170 (Assembly composition), 171 (Council composition).

leaf_note: Parliament's power to reshape States (Arts 2-4) is the classic 'unitary/federal' feature (destructible states); no Union-territory leaf exists.
micro_topic: Union and its territory > new State > First Schedule (Arts 2-4)
core_fact: Arts 2-4: a law forming a new State must amend the First Schedule (and the Fourth Schedule for Rajya Sabha seats); such a law is not an Art. 368 amendment.

statements.label: key

phrases.meaning_here: law under Art. 3, Art. 4 consequential amendments

reconstruction.correct_statement: A new State requires amendment of the First Schedule.
reconstruction.why: States are listed in Schedule I.
reconstruction.micro_topic_rule: New State: Art. 3 law -> amends Schedule I (territory) + Schedule IV (RS seats); simple majority; not Art. 368.

leaf_note: Concept of democracy underlies the nature of the Constitution.
micro_topic: Democracy > etymology
core_fact: 'Democracy' derives from Greek demos (people) + kratos (rule/power).

core_fact: Art. 45 (as substituted by the 86th Amendment 2002): the State shall endeavour to provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete six years. Original Art. 45: free and compulsory education until 14 within 10 years (now Art. 21A).
